The reaction at the centre of this investigation is between calcium carbonate (the active ingredient in Tums antacid tablets) and hydrochloric acid. The two react to form calcium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide gas, which is the bubbling that gets seen during the experiment. The balanced equation is:
2HCl(aq) + CaCO₃(s) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
This is technically an acid-carbonate reaction, which is a sub-type of acid-base neutralisation. What actually happens at the particle level is that the H⁺ ions from the dissociated HCl react with the carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) in the calcium carbonate. The first product formed is an unstable intermediate called carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which immediately decomposes into water and carbon dioxide (Libretexts, "Net Ionic Equations"). The net ionic equation for this is 2H⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(s) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), with the Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions acting as spectators. The reaction is the same one responsible for limestone erosion in acid rain, and the same one that lets Tums neutralise stomach acid (Chemistry World).
The rate of reaction is the speed at which reactants get turned into products. It is normally measured as a change in mass, volume, or concentration per unit of time. In this experiment, the rate is calculated as the mass of calcium carbonate consumed per second (g/s) by dividing the mass of CaCO₃ used in each trial by the time it took the reaction to reach its endpoint (when bubbling visibly stops).
What controls how fast any reaction goes is collision theory. According to collision theory, particles must collide with each other for any reaction to happen at all (Libretexts, "Collision Theory"). But not every collision causes a reaction. For a collision to be "effective" it needs two things: enough energy to break the bonds in the reactants, and the correct orientation when the particles meet. The minimum energy needed for a successful collision is called the activation energy (Eₐ). Anything below Eₐ and the particles just bounce off each other (MMERevise). The rate of reaction can be redefined this way as the number of successful collisions per unit time.
The independent variable is the mass of calcium carbonate. Increasing the mass of CaCO₃ added to the same fixed volume of HCl has the same kind of effect as increasing the concentration of a reactant: it puts more reactant particles into the same reaction space. Since all the Tums is pre-ground in one batch, the surface area per gram of CaCO₃ stays constant across every increment. That means a larger mass directly translates to more total surface area exposed to the acid, and more CaCO₃ particles available to collide with H⁺ ions per unit time (Sciencing, "Mass of Reactants"). The frequency of effective collisions per second goes up, so the rate of reaction should go up too (Key).
The other factors that affect rate of reaction (and that need to be controlled in this experiment) are temperature, surface area, concentration of HCl, volume of HCl, and the presence of a catalyst. Temperature affects rate because higher temperatures mean particles have more average kinetic energy. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve shifts to the right, so a larger fraction of particles end up with energy greater than Eₐ, making more collisions successful (RSC Education). Surface area matters because the reaction between a solid and a liquid only happens at the surface where the two phases meet. More surface area means more contact points, more collisions, faster reaction (Tutorchase). HCl concentration works the same way as CaCO₃ mass does: more H⁺ ions per unit volume means more collisions per unit time. Catalysts speed reactions up by offering an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, but this experiment has no catalyst (Study Mind).
The dependent variable is the time it takes for the reaction to reach its endpoint, measured in seconds with a stopwatch. The endpoint is when bubbling visibly stops, which means either all the CaCO₃ has reacted or the HCl has been used up. The DV is a reliable measure of the rate because the endpoint is observable: when CO₂ stops being produced, the reaction is done. There is some human error in deciding exactly when the bubbles stop, which is why three trials per increment are run and averaged.
Extension: this reaction is exothermic. When the H⁺ from the acid binds to the O of the carbonate to form water, strong O-H covalent bonds form. The energy released from forming those bonds is greater than the energy needed to break the original ionic bonds in the CaCO₃ and the HCl, so the system gives off heat to the surroundings (Science Ready, "Enthalpy of Neutralisation"). For strong acid + strong base reactions the standard enthalpy of neutralisation is around -57 kJ per mole of water formed, though the CaCO₃ reaction releases less because energy is also spent breaking up the carbonate lattice. The exothermic nature is why the volume of HCl is kept large enough that the small temperature rise during the reaction does not noticeably affect the rate.
